blocks.text: PROPHET OF ISRAEL IN THE DAYS OF JEROBOAM SON OF JOASH, SENT TO NINEVEH · TWO KINGDOMS
Jonah. He foretold Israel's restored borders, fled from a call to Nineveh, and preached there.
Jeroboam son of Joash · The king of Nineveh
Called, as two accounts tell it
“Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it; for their wickedness is come up before me.”
“The word of the LORD came unto Jonah”, once at the start of the book and again “the second time”. Jonah 1:1 Jonah 3:1
From the textKings gives the outcome of his word to Jeroboam's Israel but not its words. 2 Kings 14:25
In Nineveh his preaching is given as one sentence: “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.” Jonah 3:4
He prayed from the fish's belly, and prayed again in anger when Nineveh was spared; the LORD answered him with questions. Jonah 2:1–9 Jonah 4:2–4 Jonah 4:9–11
“He restored the coast of Israel from the entering of Hamath unto the sea of the plain”
“Who can tell if God will turn and repent, and turn away from his fierce anger, that we perish not?”
The word in its main themes
“Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.”
“And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil, that he had said that he would do unto them; and he did it not.”
“I cried by reason of mine affliction unto the LORD, and he heard me”
“for I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repentest thee of the evil.”
“And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and also much cattle?”
To whom the word was spoken
“I am an Hebrew; and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, which hath made the sea and the dry land.”
“Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.”
The gourd, the worm and the east wind
1 The call and the flight to sea Jonah 1:1–16
2 The great fish and Jonah's prayer Jonah 1:17–2:10
4 Jonah's anger and the gourd Jonah 4:1–11
WHERE THE NEW TESTAMENT QUOTES IT · 3
Each band joins a chapter of Jonah to the New Testament books quoting it (2 books).
Who stood with him, and against him
From the textThe book ends with the LORD's question, “should not I spare Nineveh”, and no answer from Jonah. Scripture says nothing of him afterwards, nor of his death. Jonah 4:9–11

Jesus answered those who asked for a sign: “there shall no sign be given to it, but the sign of the prophet Jonas: For as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.” Matthew 12:38–40

“The men of Nineveh shall rise in judgment with this generation, and shall condemn it: because they repented at the preaching of Jonas; and, behold, a greater than Jonas is here.” Matthew 12:41 Luke 11:32
Luke: “as Jonas was a sign unto the Ninevites, so shall also the Son of man be to this generation.” Matthew gives “the sign of the prophet Jonas” a second time. Luke 11:29–30 Matthew 16:4

A Jewish tradition reported by Jerome made Jonah the son of the widow of Zarephath whom Elijah raised; Keil calls it “nothing more than a Jewish Hagada”. 1 Kings 17:17–24 [3][14] Who says so: Jerome, preface to his commentary on Jonah, as reported by C. F. Keil (tr. 1868), about AD 395–397 (the 1893 translators give both years)

Keil reports a grave of Jonah shown at Meshad in Galilee and another at Nineveh, and gives them no more weight than the Zarephath story.[3] Who says so: As reported by C. F. Keil (tr. 1868), shown in the 19th century; the earliest source is not given
E. B. Pusey (1860s; printing of 1869), pp. 248, 255; C. F. Keil (tr. 1868), pp. 380–388; J. R. Sampey (ISBE 1915), who names Keil, Pusey, Delitzsch, Orelli and J. Kennedy as holding it

Pusey writes that “Our Lord relates it as a fact”. Keil argues that Jonah's three days could be a type of Christ's death and resurrection only if they had “as much objective reality as the facts of the death, burial, and resurrection of Christ”, and so the book “relates historical facts”. Matthew 12:40–41 [4][3][7]
A teaching story on a basis of fact

Driver finds “indications that it is not strictly historical” and a chiefly “didactic purpose”, but holds that the materials “rest ultimately upon a basis of fact” and that Jonah's preaching at Nineveh was successful, “though not upon the scale represented in the book”. Jonah 3:5–10 [5]

Smith writes that the book does not “claim to be real history” but “offers to us all the marks of the parable or allegory”: the three days in the fish, the general account of Nineveh's conversion, and the abrupt close once the moral is plain. Jonah 1:17 Jonah 3:5 Jonah 4:11 [6]
An allegory of Israel's exile and return
O. Kleinert, T. K. Cheyne and C. H. H. Wright (as reported by Driver, 1891, p. 304)

On this view, as Driver summarises it, Jonah stands for Israel, which shrank from its calling, was “swallowed up” by Babylon and brought back, and then was disappointed that judgement on the nations did not come. Jonah 1:3 Jonah 1:17 Jonah 4:1 [5]
2 Kings 14 Jonah 1 Jonah 2 Jonah 3 Jonah 4 Matthew 12 Matthew 16 Luke 11
Kings does not record the words of Jonah's prophecy to Jeroboam's Israel, only what came of it.
The book does not name the king of Nineveh, say where the fish cast Jonah up, or say what Jonah did after the LORD's last question.
Scripture does not say when or where Jonah died.
The book does not say that Jonah wrote it; it speaks of him in the third person.
